text: Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?

title: Summary
text:
Survey details
Community forest management (CFM) has expanded rapidly in Zambia since receiving enabling regulations in 2018. As of January 2025, 351 Community Forest Management Groups (CFMGs) preside over approximately 9.4 million hectares of community forests across all ten provinces.
In contrast to many other countries where CFM involves transfer of primarily domestic user rights for forest products, Zambia’s legal framework provides the lawful transfer of exclusive economic rights over forest resources to CFMGs. This means communities gain not only the right to use and manage their forest, but also the right to benefit from economic activities, including markets for ecosystem services. The opportunity to participate in voluntary carbon markets has made Zambia an attractive destination for carbon finance and climate-focused investment. The combination of secure tenure and carbon income potential has driven a rapid expansion of CFM with most of the 351 CFMGs having been established in the past three years, often with significant external investment and technical support from carbon developers or conservation partners. However, this also represents a significant vulnerability. The rapid expansion has been substantially fuelled by external investment rather than by domestic government commitments. If carbon markets contract or if carbon developers reduce their engagement, CFM expansion could slow markedly and existing CFMGs could face sustainability challenges without diversified income streams or consistent government support.
This report presents findings from a survey of 80 CFMGs conducted across eight provinces in 2024. The two provinces omitted — Luapula and Copperbelt — had very few CFMGs at the time of the survey. Five CFMGs included in the original sample were found to be defunct and so were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 75 CFMGs. The sample spans a wide range of community forest area (CFA) sizes (from approximately 20 ha to over 80,000 ha) and ages (from one to approximately seven years since establishment; age distribution), and reflects the national age structure of the programme, in which most CFAs are fewer than three years old.
The survey employed a multi-perspective focus group discussion (FGD) design. Four structured FGDs were conducted at each CFA: with the CFMG executive committee, community men, community women and community youth (survey coverage). This design enables the systematic comparison of perspectives across stakeholder groups. Near-complete coverage of all four FGD types across the 75 CFAs means that differences in responses among groups can be interpreted with confidence. Individual interviews were conducted with CFMG executive members, District Forest Officers (DFOs), traditional leaders, forest user-group chairs and external partners (e.g. conservation NGOs, carbon developers, NTFP off-takers), providing an additional layer of evidence from a range of vantage points.
The geographic spread of the sample — covering Northwestern, Western, Lusaka, Northern, Muchinga, Eastern, Southern and Central provinces (coverage by province) — ensures that findings reflect diverse ecological, economic and socio-political contexts. The gender breakdown of interviewees is male-biased, as expected given that men dominate most CFMG stakeholder roles. However, the dedicated female FGD conducted in each CFA ensured that women’s perspectives were systematically captured.
In short, the sample provides a robust, nationally representative foundation for drawing inferences about CFM implementation in Zambia. The multi-perspective design is particularly well suited to examining the governance and equity dimensions of CFM, which are among the most important — and most contested — aspects of the programme.

title: Summary
text:
Governance
The governance of CFMGs is assessed across five domains: legal processes, governance processes (elections, meetings, financial management), business processes (workplans, budgets, business plans), external support, and community buy-in. The most consistent pattern across all three process domains is that foundational steps have been taken by most CFMGs, but the more demanding requirements are frequently incomplete.
Legal processes are the most advanced domain. A large majority of CFMGs in the sample have obtained a recognition letter and signed a forest management agreement — the foundational steps for establishing a CFA (legal process completion). However, later and more administratively demanding processes, including the registration certificate, forest-use permit and benefit-sharing agreement, are absent in a substantial proportion. These are not minor procedural details: without a registration certificate and forest-use permit, a CFMG’s legal basis for managing its forest and excluding external actors is weakened, and its ability to negotiate with carbon buyers and other commercial partners is compromised.
Governance processes are more unevenly implemented. Most CFMGs have held at least one election and have term limits for executive officers (election frequency), and most hold CFMG meetings with reasonable frequency. However, several basic management actions are missing in a large proportion of CFMGs: bank accounts have not been opened, receipt books are not maintained, and annual financial and technical reports are rarely produced (governance process rates). Again, these are not peripheral concerns. Without bank accounts, carbon payments and other income cannot be transparently managed. Without receipt books and financial reporting, there is no basis for demonstrating accountability to community members or external partners. The fact that most CFMGs are overdue for elections is of particular concern. Timely elections are a basic requirement of the CFMG by-laws and overdue elections undermine legitimacy. In some cases, this appears to reflect deliberate retention of control in anticipation of carbon income.
Business processes are the weakest domain. Annual workplans, budgets and business plans are present in only a minority of CFMGs (business process rates). Without these planning and financial management tools, CFMGs are poorly positioned to manage resources sustainably, account for income or sustain compliance with their forest management license.
External support presents a mixed picture. Most CFMGs are rarely or never visited by DFOs, despite the statutory duty of the FD to implement the CFM policy (DFO visit frequency). This gap is partly compensated by conservation NGOs and carbon developers, many of which visit their partner CFMGs regularly. However, this support is not universal: a significant proportion of CFMGs in the sample had no external partner of any kind (external partner coverage). Where NGO or carbon developer support is present, it has funded real improvements in forest management — patrol systems, fire management and agricultural extension. The current model, in which CFM is effectively co-governed by the community and the private sector, may be adequate where active and capable partners are present, but leaves many CFMGs without meaningful support.
Interest in expanding the community forest, which is used as an indicator of community satisfaction with CFM, is highest among CFMG executives and lowest among community youth (interest in expansion by stakeholder group). Among individual interviewees, NGO representatives are significantly more enthusiastic about expansion than traditional leaders or community members. This divergence — consistent with the equity findings discussed below — suggests that CFMG leadership and external partners have a more optimistic assessment of CFM outcomes than the broader community. If not addressed, this gap risks eroding legitimacy and the long-term sustainability of CFM.
In summary, CFMG governance is still maturing. The legal framework for CFM is largely in place, but institutional and business management processes lag behind. Strengthening financial management, ensuring timely elections, expanding district forestry staff engagement and closing the gap between executive and community perspectives are essential to secure the future of CFM in Zambia.

title: Summary
text:
Sustainable Forest Management
Across all SFM indicators, the evidence points to meaningful improvements under CFM. Clear majorities of community FGD groups report that deforestation has decreased (reduced deforestation), charcoal production has declined, fire frequency has fallen (reduced fire) and wildlife populations have increased (wildlife recovery) within their CFA. These are substantial changes given that, for most communities, CFM has been operating for fewer than five years.
Importantly, the large majority of FGD groups also report that deforestation and charcoal production are decreasing in areas outside their community forest (deforestation outside CFA). This indicates that CFM is not simply displacing pressure from CFAs into adjacent landscapes, but is actually generating broader environmental benefits in the surrounding area.
Community female FGD groups tend to report change in SFM outcomes more positively than other FGD types — a pattern that recurs across multiple indicators and domains. This may reflect that women, who are traditionally highly dependent on forest resources for household provisioning but have historically had limited say in management decisions, have gained meaningful voice through CFM’s formal governance structures. However, to confirm this would require further research.
Among individual interviewees, DFOs and NGO representatives tend to report somewhat more conservative assessments of positive change than community members. This may reflect a broader professional perspective on forest management, or it may reflect that these professionals are less aware of the day-to-day improvements visible to those living adjacent to the CFA. Longer-term monitoring will be required to better understand these CFM outcomes.
Restoration activities — protection of natural regeneration and, in a few cases, planting — are occurring in some CFMGs, but are not widespread (restoration uptake). Given the Zambian government’s restoration commitments and the central role that CFM could play in delivering them, this is a significant missed opportunity. A dedicated restoration component — covering natural regeneration, and planting of native and, where appropriate, exotic species — should be integrated into forest management plans for all CFMGs. Similarly, agroforestry and timber plantation establishment, which could both reduce pressure on natural forests and generate valuable additional income streams, were practised by only a small number of CFMGs.
In summary, CFM in Zambia is driving real improvements in SFM across a large majority of surveyed communities. However, these improvements are not ubiquitous. Critically, governance quality (as captured by our governance index) was a significant predictor of how positively respondents viewed SFM outcomes. Identifying under-performing CFMGs, diagnosing the causes and implementing corrective action will be essential. Equally, integrating restoration, plantation and agroforestry components into the CFM model would substantially strengthen its contribution to national SFM targets.

title: Summary
text:
Remote Sensing analysis
The remote sensing analysis provides independent, satellite-based evidence on three key indicators of CFM effectiveness: fire incidence, deforestation rates and changes in above-ground biomass (AGB). The analysis uses a before-after design that compares outcomes within CFA cores before and after establishment, and with buffer zones as a spatial control and assessment of leakage.
Across all three fire metrics — fire detection density (Figure), burned area fraction (Figure) and fire radiative power (Figure) — there were statistically significant reductions within CFA cores following establishment. These results constitute robust, multi-indicator satellite confirmation that CFM has led to meaningful improvements in fire management at within the CFA. Importantly, fires in buffer areas also declined, indicating improvements at the landscape scale. These results are consistent with community perceptions documented in the SFM chapter, where a clear majority of FGD groups reported that fire frequency was declining both inside and outside their CFA.
According to the Hansen Global Forest Canopy dataset, tree cover loss rates within CFA cores did not change significantly following establishment (tree cover loss). Although the directional trend was in the right direction, the change was statistically modest. This result may initially appear contradictory given the strongly positive community perceptions, but several explanations are plausible. First, baseline deforestation rates within CFA cores were already very low (median of approximately 0.14% per year) before establishment, leaving limited scope for measurable further decline. Second, tree cover data are often unreliable at small spatial scales in miombo woodlands, where canopy cover is naturally sparse and assessments can vary seasonally due to the relative strength of the grass versus tree canopy signal. Third, communities may be perceiving real improvements through indirect indicators — such as reduced charcoal production, fewer incursions or recovery of the forest understorey — that are not captured by the canopy loss metric. According to the Hansen dataset there was a significant increase in tree cover loss in the 1 km buffer zones (from a median of 0.26% before CFA establishment to 0.49% afterwards) around CFAs. However, this should be interpreted cautiously given the measurement reliability issues noted above. Continued monitoring over a longer period or development of miombo specific tree cover analyses are recommended, before making solid conclusions.
The fact that our analysis detected very low rates of deforestation in CFAs prior to establishment is concerning. Although our analysis was based on a small sample and a relatively short observation window, we would have expected a higher rate of deforestation before establishment and a significant reduction in that rate following establishment. It is difficult to see from our results how carbon developers can be justifying any meaningful additionality from their projects. Moving to a jurisdictional approach will be essential to maintain confidence in Zambian carbon.
Above-ground biomass increased significantly in both CFA cores and buffer zones following CFMG establishment (above-ground biomass). For dry seasonal forests such as the miombo woodlands that dominate Zambia’s community forests, biomass is likely a more sensitive and reliable indicator of ecological condition than canopy cover loss. Biomass monitoring can detect incremental changes caused by shifts in tree recruitment and growth, which are not captured by canopy cover metrics. The observed biomass gains are consistent with — and likely substantially attributable to — the documented reductions in fire disturbance. Fire both kills trees directly and suppresses woody recruitment. Even modest reductions in annual burning can produce measurable biomass accumulation in a few years.
In summary, the remote sensing evidence presents a nuanced but largely positive picture of CFM effectiveness. CFM has demonstrably reduced fire disturbance and produced measurable gains in above-ground biomass across both CFAs and in their immediate surroundings. Canopy cover was stable within CFAs, but may be decreasing in the buffer areas around CFAs — further monitoring of the situation is advised. While CFM may increase protection of CFAs, the economic drivers of deforestation — primarily charcoal production and agricultural clearance — are not directly addressed by CFM at larger spatial scales and require other interventions.

title: Summary
text:
Economic transformation
The economic outcomes of CFM are real but narrowly distributed, and the full potential remains largely untapped. The analysis covers five domains: access to forest resources, employment, carbon income, non-timber forest products and other income-generating activities, and opportunity costs.
Most FGD groups and individual interviewees indicate that CFM has not increased access to natural resources for either household use or sale. This is perhaps unsurprising, as communities were harvesting forest products before CFM was established. However, approximately one third of respondent groups felt that access had improved, likely reflecting the formalisation of community rights and establishment of user-groups.
Employment has grown under CFM (employment by FGD group), but the picture is more complicated than the headline numbers suggest. The most significant employment gains are in the roles of Honorary Forest Officers (HFOs) and community scouts — positions that are low-paying and predominantly male. Community female FGD groups were the most likely to report no change in formal employment and community youth groups were the most likely to report gains — a difference that likely reflects the demographics of the HFO and community scout roles. While new employment is a genuine achievement, the scale and quality of that employment currently falls well short of what a thriving forest-based economy should deliver.
Carbon income is the centrepiece of the CFM economic model in Zambia, and its impact is significant where it has materialised. Approximately one third of CFMG communities in the sample had received carbon payments at the time of the survey (carbon finance by province). The activities funded by carbon developers — patrol systems, fire management, climate-smart agriculture extension — also represent a injection of capital into forest margin communities. However, the fact that a substantial number of community youth FGD groups were unaware of carbon agreements (carbon awareness by FGD group) is concerning. It suggests that carbon developers may not have conducted a fully inclusive FPIC process and that CFMG executives may not be communicating adequately with their communities. This information asymmetry is a governance risk that could erode community support for CFM over time.
Beyond carbon and honey, the economic potential of Zambia’s community forests is almost entirely untapped. A wide variety of forest products are harvested from community forests — including timber, wild fruits, medicinal plants, mushrooms, caterpillars, bamboo, resins and thatching grass — but overwhelmingly for household use or local sale with minimal value addition. Only a small number of CFMGs (15%) are partnering with any kind of enterprise (enterprise collaboration), and where they are, it is almost exclusively for honey. The communities themselves identify a rich diversity of products — prominently including timber and wild fruits as well as mushrooms and honey — that could be developed into community enterprises (unrealised opportunities). The potential to layer multiple income streams on top of one another, supply urban and regional markets with value-added products, and create more stable income for community members is substantial. CFM has the legal and institutional scaffolding to support this kind of diversified forest economy. What is lacking is the investment, technical support and market linkages needed to activate it.
Opportunity costs of CFM — foregone income, restricted access to previously used areas, time and resource costs of participation — are recognised by communities (opportunity costs by FGD group), and are important to acknowledge. Opportunity costs fall most heavily on households that were most dependent on forest clearing or other activities that are now restricted, and these households are disproportionately among the most economically vulnerable. Properly accounting for and mitigating opportunity costs — including through explicit provision in benefit-sharing arrangements and business plans — should be a standard part of CFMG management.
In summary, CFM has achieved real but limited economic transformation. The economic model currently relies too heavily on carbon and a single NTFP (honey), leaving most communities with a narrow income base that is vulnerable to market fluctuations and partner decisions. A more diversified economic model — one that exploits the full range of forest products, develops community enterprises, and actively links communities to urban, regional and international markets — is both achievable and necessary.

title: Summary
text:
Equity and Inclusion
The equity and inclusion chapter investigates a wide range of outcomes: benefit sharing, opportunity costs, gender equity, transparency, grievance and redress, and poverty impacts. The overarching finding is that equity outcomes under CFM are broadly positive, but the picture is uneven and contains important warning signals.
The most striking pattern across all equity indicators is a systematic divergence in perspective by FGD group. Community female and youth groups consistently report more negative assessments of equity outcomes than CFMG executive and community male groups — across virtually every indicator, including equitable benefit sharing (Figure), women benefiting from CFM (Figure), women’s participation in decision making (Figure), and transparency in benefit sharing (Figure). This divergence could reflect information asymmetries. CFMG executives, who are better informed about formal governance arrangements, may genuinely perceive a more equitable distribution than is visible to other community members. Alternatively — and perhaps more plausibly — it may reflect that the benefits and costs of CFM are in fact distributed unevenly, in ways that are visible to those outside the executive circle but not acknowledged by those within it. Furthermore, elite capture and corruption cannot be ruled out in a subset of cases.
Notwithstanding these concerns, the overall picture is more positive than might have been expected. A clear majority of all FGD groups — including community female groups — report that benefits are being shared equitably and that women benefit from CFM. Most female groups state that women do not disproportionately bear opportunity costs and that women participate in CFM decision making. This is an encouraging finding in a country where natural resource management has traditionally been the purview of male community members. The formal governance structures mandated by CFM — including elections, executive positions with required female representation, documented benefit-sharing arrangements, and formation of user-groups — may have given women a degree of recognition and voice that they did not previously have. In this respect, CFM may have served as a tool for institutional gender mainstreaming in forest management. However, the impacts of CFM on gender equity requires further study to understand the conditions around positive and negative outcomes.
Community youth groups present a consistently more critical perspective across all domains. Youth are the most sceptical about CFM’s benefits, the most concerned about elite capture and transparency, and the most likely to report that CFM has not delivered meaningful livelihood improvements for their demographic. The formalisation of CFM may have worked against youth empowerment to a degree by entrenching control by older community members who dominate community management bodies, such as CFMGs. Unless addressed, youth dissatisfaction poses a genuine long-term risk to community support for CFM.
Carbon benefit-sharing agreements are structured almost entirely around revenue sharing with little provision for employment, infrastructure investment or targeted livelihood support, other than climate smart agriculture. While revenue sharing delivers a direct financial return when payments materialise, communities that have not yet received payments — which is the majority — have little tangible benefit to show. Diversifying the components of company-community agreements to include employment targets, skills development, and livelihood support would broaden both the distribution of benefits and community buy-in across diverse stakeholder groups.
The poverty impacts of CFM — primarily through increased household incomes and new income-generating activities (poverty impact) — are broadly consistent with the economic transformation findings. They are real but very limited, and the barriers that prevent the most vulnerable households from benefiting, such as low social capital and sometimes physical capacity (e.g. learning disabled or physically disabled) are structural and will require deliberate policy attention to overcome.
In summary, CFM appears to have made meaningful progress on equity and inclusion, particularly with respect to women’s voice in forest management. However, the divergence between the perspectives of community female and youth groups on one side and CFMG executives and males on the other is the most important equity signal from this survey. Strengthening transparency, grievance and redress mechanisms, ensuring that youth groups are meaningfully engaged in benefit sharing, establishing programmes for the most vulnerable community members and monitoring for elite capture are essential to ensuring CFM delivers equitable outcomes across the full diversity of community stakeholders.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?
Derived from our findings, we make the recommendations detailed below. We attempt to cover all the key changes that need to be made to improve CFM implementation in Zambia and we structure our recommendations around the same four domains that the report focuses on, namely governance, SFM, economic transformation and equity and inclusion. We acknowledge that others may have made similar recommendations and we also note that efforts may already be in place to address some of the issues. However, our purpose here is to provide a comprehensive set of recommendations that arise from our work.
The recommendations below are intended for three key audiences. We indicate the primary intended audience: [GRZ] for government policymakers, [FD] for Forestry Department managers and district-level facilitators, and [Practitioners] for NGOs, carbon developers, and other development partners. Many recommendations are cross-cutting and relevant to multiple audiences.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Governance
High quality governance is essential to CFM. The state, through the Forestry Department, must provide adequate oversight to ensure CFM regulations are being followed and the agreed upon forest management plans implemented. CFMGs must comply with their own constitutions, implement financial and management actions transparently, and ensure equitable benefit sharing, as well as functioning grievance and redress processes. Private entities, such as carbon developers and conservation NGOs, must implement FPIC processes properly and ensure their actions support CFMGs in implementing good governance.

Institutional Capacity and Oversight

[GRZ, FD] The FD should establish a national CFM unit to support implementation. This unit should focus on capacity development for forestry staff, so they are able to support CFM at the provincial and district level. In addition, forestry curricular for tertiary institutions, such as Copperbelt University and the Zambia Forestry College, need to be updated so that graduates are trained in CFM.



Monitoring and Compliance Tracking

[FD] Transition the current CFM database into a digital management dashboard for CFM monitoring that can be integrated with digital data collection tools and file uploads. Ideally, this dashboard would have an associated App that would facilitate recording of data on common processes, such as CFMG meetings and elections, permits, workplans, budgets, annual reports, and so on. Information on compliance could be displayed using a traffic light system, which would enable district staff to quickly identify CFMGs requiring prioritized support and mentoring, and would provide an objective basis for tackling elite capture through improved transparency and accountability. Tracking CFM compliance is complicated and requires timely access to evidence collected through monitoring. Hence, the Forestry Department should make maximum use of digital tools to facilitate this process. Furthermore, these tools and information systems should be made available in multiple local languages to ensure accessibility across communities with varying literacy levels in English, and capacity-development for using these systems should be continuous and adaptive, incorporating feedback from users to improve monitoring approaches over time.
[FD] District forest office staff should be required to visit CFMGs once per quarter and support the CFMGs in developing and implementing their budgets and workplans, as well as ensuring they are compliant with their constitutions and national regulations with respect to reporting, holding meetings and elections. They should be applying the “Checklists – CFM Step 7: Joint Monitoring, Evaluation and Lesson Learning”. CFM Step 7 serves as a critical quality assurance mechanism, verifying that CFMGs are fulfilling their obligations to protect, control access and manage their forests according to agreed management plans. Step 7 assessments also highlight gaps in earlier implementation steps (FPIC, boundary conflicts, user identification, constitution development, rules and sanctions, permits and fees). Key Performance Indicators for district office staff should be adjusted to reflect their role in the delivery of CFM support, with quarterly CFMG visits and reports as a measurable target.
[GRZ, FD] Develop explicit performance standards for CFM implementation. While national guidelines provide recommended processes and expected outputs, formal performance standards should be established to enable monitoring of CFMG capacity and service provider performance. These standards should cover: (i) governance processes (elections, meetings, financial management); (ii) forest management actions (boundary maintenance, patrols, fire prevention); (iii) sustainable harvest of forest products; and (iv) benefit sharing and equity outcomes. Reference the example of performance standards developed for Participatory Forestry in Malawi, which enabled consistent monitoring across multiple CFA service providers and projects. Performance standards should be integrated into the monitoring dashboard and used to guide capacity building and support.



Private Sector Engagement

[GRZ, Practitioners] Carbon developers and conservation NGOs should be required to provide support to CFMGs as a component of their business plans. The types of support should be standardised through regulations and guidelines, and should include support in CFMG governance compliance, forest management and enterprise development.



Budget and Financing

[GRZ, FD] Funds need to be made available for regular district forest office staff visits to CFMGs and for implementation of improved monitoring and compliance systems. The financial justification for this investment can be framed in several ways: (i) CFAs function as long-term concession areas for community exclusive use, comparable to active timber concessions where the Forestry Department provides oversight — the same logic justifies investment in CFM oversight; (ii) the Forest Development Fund (established under Section 70(3) of the Forests Act, 2015) has explicit provision for promotion of community-based forest management practices, providing a potential domestic funding source; and (iii) the government’s carbon business plan should include a component for supporting improved CFMG governance as a necessary condition for realizing carbon revenues at scale. A portion of government revenue from carbon should be ear-marked specifically for CFM support, creating a dedicated funding stream.



Standardization and Transparency

[FD] The appointment of district forest enterprise officers is a step in the right direction. However, these officers also need training, so that they can support the establishment and management of community-based forest product enterprises. The Forestry Department should work in tandem with the National Forest Commodities Association to develop models and associated training packs for different forest product value chains. Forestry enterprise officers should then be trained to deliver the capacity building required for each of these models.
[FD] In line with the “Checklists – CFM Step 7: Joint Monitoring, Evaluation and Lesson Learning” implementation, increased standardisation of important CFMG processes would expedite compliance, simplify monitoring and reduce the risk of poor outcomes. Standardisation should cover: (i) election processes, tenure and term limits for CFMG members and executive positions; (ii) financial processes, including opening bank accounts, maintaining receipt books, payments to employees including HFOs, and gratuities to CFMG members and executives for participating in activities; (iii) reporting requirements, including presentation of annual financial and activity reports to community members; (iv) grievance and redress mechanisms; and (v) benefit sharing arrangements for both carbon and other CFMG income. A number of these are already in the standard CFM agreement, but implementation is patchy, and many could be standardised to a much greater degree. Where more flexibility is required, the FD should publish guidelines, such as for different permitting arrangements and user-group management.
[FD] To improve transparency and accountability, require publishing of decisions made at CFMG meetings and posting of these around the community. Minutes of CFMG meetings should also be uploaded to the FD’s CFM database. Transparency in decision-making is a key governance marker and essential to addressing elite capture and ensuring equitable benefit sharing.
[FD] Require that the district forest office staff and CFMG executives sign off on annual budgets and workplans by a specified date and submit them to the FD CFM database. This creates accountability on both sides and ensures baseline documentation for monitoring.



User Group Registration and CFMG-Enterprise Relationship

[FD] Require registration and permitting of all forest user-groups, even if these are community groups and there is no intention to charge a permit fee. Formalising forest use and agreeing on management protocols, such as start dates and off-take levels, is essential for SFM.
[FD, Practitioners] We recommend separating the role of CFMGs from income generating activities. CFMGs should focus on their core regulatory function — protecting, controlling access to and managing the forest according to agreed plans — while user groups and community-based forest enterprises operate as income-generating entities. This separation clarifies incentives, reduces role conflict, improves transparency, and enables the FD to better monitor CFMG compliance with forest management obligations. The relationship between CFMGs and enterprises should be clarified in forest management plans and user group agreements.
[FD] Community-based forest enterprises should be explicitly tracked in the FD database and distinguished from the regulatory role of CFMGs. They should be set up as cooperatives or as businesses under the Patents and Companies Registration Agency (PACRA) with community shareholders.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Sustainable Forest Management
Sustainable forest management is one of the key objectives of CFM. Ensuring that CFMGs are taking management actions to protect and manage their forest resources is, therefore, essential. Boundary marking, patrolling by HFOs, fire prevention and other actions such as planting and restoration require annual budgets and workplans. Communities need to monitor boundary incursions and fire incidence, and track NTFP off-take, as well as record any transgressions of by-laws, such as forest clearance or tree cutting, and track the actions taken against the perpetrators, such as fines.

[FD] The district forest office staff and CFMGs should identify key SFM activities within the management plan and annual workplans and budgets — such as boundary marking, fire monitoring and patrolling — with completion dates for key milestones. These plans should be uploaded to the FD’s CFM database for monitoring. Progress on key SFM milestones should be tracked and reported through the national CFM dashboard.
[FD] Annual reports should have a standardised format that includes reporting on SFM activities, linked to key milestones set in the annual workplans. This will enable comparison across CFMGs and aggregation at provincial and national levels.
[GRZ, FD] CFM is a key mechanism for the government to deliver on restoration commitments, but currently this is not being adequately implemented or assessed. CFA boundaries should encompass areas that have restoration potential, such as areas that have been cleared or degraded through fire or charcoal production. The suitability of areas for restoration should also consider the ecosystem service delivery potential, such as watershed protection. CFMGs should identify restoration sites within the CFA in forest management plans. Any area that is substantially degraded when the CFA was established may be considered a restoration site. Within restoration sites, the management plan should identify areas for (i) natural regeneration (protection only) or (ii) planting with indigenous species or exotic species. If planting is planned, a business plan for harvesting the timber or other products should be developed to justify the investment.
[FD, Practitioners] Establish community-based monitoring systems for NTFPs. The design of these systems should be standardised by the FD, so that data can be collected and aggregated at the national scale. However, monitoring should be implemented by the community using digital tools, and feed into a FD managed digital platform, with a dashboard for community viewing. The design of these monitoring systems should incorporate traditional knowledge held by community members about NTFP species, sustainable harvest seasons, and resource dynamics, and combined with scientific monitoring protocols to develop culturally-appropriate and effective approaches. Ideally, this dashboard would be integrated with the national CFM monitoring dashboard, rather than separate from it.
[GRZ, FD] The FD should consider a small plantation programme or outgrowers schemes for CFAs for timber and sustainable charcoal production. These could be established on deforested land within the CFA and would contribute to Zambia’s plantation and timber production targets.
[GRZ, FD] We found that deforestation rates prior to CFA establishment were very low, although >80% of CFAs were established to generate carbon credits. This raises the possibility that carbon developers are exaggerating the climate change mitigation potential of their interventions. Zambia is already trialling approaches for establishing a jurisdictional approach for carbon accounting, and these results suggest it should be rolled out across the country as soon as possible to maintain credibility in Zambian carbon.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Economic transformation
The economic development of local communities through forest-based enterprises is, together with SFM, the other major objective of CFM. However, most community forest resource use, aside from charcoal, is for household consumption or perhaps for sale through local markets with little to no value addition. Through CFM, carbon finance has brought some local investment and direct income, but the substantial opportunity for developing enterprises around other forest resources is largely going to waste. For the Zambia government to realise its ambition for economic development through CFM, a much greater investment in supporting the establishment and management of community enterprises is required.

Market Development and Knowledge Support

[GRZ, FD, Practitioners] The Forestry Department, in collaboration with the National Forest Commodities Association and other partners, should establish a national knowledge hub on forest product management, value addition, and marketing. It should help promote forest product innovation through research and technical support, and connect producers with buyers by organising forest product exhibitions at, for example, the annual agricultural shows at provincial and national levels.



Capacity Development

[FD] Provide capacity development to district forest enterprise officers. They should receive training in management and value addition for forest product value chains, business skills and financial management.
[FD] District forest enterprise officers should be required to provide capacity support for, at minimum, two forest value chains per CFMG. They should provide capacity development training for user-group members, and support them in business management, such as in financial management and reporting. KPIs should require quarterly visits to each CFA and documented capacity building activities.



Diversification and Market Access

[Practitioners] To address the lack of diversity in forest product economic activities, encourage carbon developers and NGOs working with CFMGs to include a minimum of two forest product value chains in each CFA as a standard component of partnership agreements.
[FD] Require the production and submission to FD of business plans for CFAs. These plans should be submitted alongside (or be a part of) the forest management plans that are required for CFA establishment. The format should be standardised to facilitate the maintenance of quality and so that comparable data can be extracted from them.
[FD, Practitioners] Require community monitoring of harvested quantities of forest products for household use and for sale, using digital tools as described in the SFM section above. Data should be aggregated to assess sustainability of off-take levels and to identify emerging economic opportunities.
[FD] Require recording of employment statistics, such as types of jobs and hours worked per month, as a component of the community monitoring. This will enable tracking of employment creation and identification of opportunities to improve job quality.
[GRZ, FD, Practitioners] Develop a programme for community-based eco-tourism through CFAs and their intersection with national heritage sites. This should build on experiences at existing community-based eco-tourism sites, such as the M’panshya Campsite in Rufunsa and those run by Frankfurt Zoological Society in the North Luangwa landscape. CFM offers an opportunity to protect, and potentially restore, the environment around national heritage sites, while simultaneous promoting an eco-tourism enterprise to support income generation. The National Heritage Conservation Commission has a mandate to work with communities at national heritage sites, so there is a clear opportunity for collaboration between the Ministry of Tourism and the MoGEE in realising a common goal.



Forest Certification

[FD, Practitioners] Consider promoting Forest Stewardship Certification (FSC) for CFMGs, but with realistic expectations. FSC certification can improve carbon credit values by up to 100% and open international markets for NTFPs. However, transaction costs for individual CFMG certification can be high. Hence, a group certification approach may be more cost-effective, which could be implemented through the FD if their monitoring and oversight of CFM is sufficient to ensure FSC compliance. Any FSC initiative should be paired with capacity building to ensure CFMGs can meet certification requirements.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Equity and inclusion
Equity and inclusion is a critical component of the social and economic development that should be achieved through CFM. First, the democratic processes involved in CFM, such as representation through the CFMG and participation in forest user-groups, give a voice to community members who might otherwise not be heard. Specific stipulations in the CFMG constitution can promote this further by requiring, for example, women or youth representatives on the CFMG and its executive. Second, forest resources often provide a safety-net for vulnerable community members, for example, by providing food resources at times of year when they experience seasonal hunger. Again, through representation, CFM can ensure these resources and the access rights of vulnerable community members are protected and also provide opportunities for vulnerable community members to participate in forest resource-based enterprises. However, with poor governance there are risks of elite capture and further marginalisation of vulnerable community members by excluding them from accessing essential forest resources. Hence, oversight of equity and inclusion provisions and their implementation is essential.

[FD, Practitioners] Require identification of opportunity costs of CFM and the community members most negatively affected in the forest management plan, and require a mitigation plan for the impacts of these opportunity costs. This should be a specific component of the forest management plan and monitored through the national CFM database.
[FD, Practitioners] Require consideration of vulnerable groups in the designation of forest user-groups and in the benefit-sharing arrangements. User-group formation should explicitly address participation by vulnerable households, including the elderly, people with disabilities, and those with limited social capital.
[FD, Practitioners] Encourage and support development of women’s and youth forest product enterprises. These could be supported through dedicated funding, capacity building, and market linkages to ensure that benefits from CFM reach beyond traditional power-holders.

title: Introduction
text:
Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?






Community forestry
Community forest management (CFM) has emerged over the past five decades as a dominant paradigm in forest governance, grounded in the recognition that local communities — as the de facto managers over large areas of the world’s forests — are best placed to sustainably manage the resources on which they depend. At its core, CFM involves the formal transfer of management authority and resource use rights, including the right to benefit from the sale of forest resources, from state institutions to local communities [@charnley2007; @fao1978]. Early programmes in the 1970s and 1980s focused narrowly on fuelwood supply and tree planting in South Asia and the Sahel, but CFM has since evolved into a broad and diverse set of approaches — including participatory forest management, joint forest management, and community-based forest management — implemented across Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe [@roberts2003; @bray2005; @colfer2010a; @baynes2015; @gilmour2016].
The rationale for CFM rests on the premise that local communities, with vested interests in maintaining forest resource flows and access to place- and time-specific knowledge, can govern forests more effectively and sustainably than centralised state institutions, especially where the state has limited resources to enforce forest management regulations [@hajjar2021]. Where well-implemented, CFM has delivered substantive benefits: forest regeneration (by as much as 37% in Nepal), reduced deforestation, enhanced biodiversity conservation, improved rural livelihoods and incomes, and stronger local institutions and community cohesion [@gilmour2016; @charnley2007; @baynes2015]. Community forestry also positions local communities to participate in emerging carbon, biodiversity and ecosystem service markets, offering new revenue streams for forest protection.
Nevertheless, the outcomes of CFM globally have been mixed [@roberts2003]. Recurring challenges include weak institutional capacity, insecure land tenure, unclear forest boundaries and competing resource claims, inequitable benefit-sharing arrangements, limited social capital, governance capacity and business acumen among local communities, and poor market access [@wily2004; @mcdermott2009]. The conditions most conducive to CFM success include a sound legal framework devolving management and user rights to communities, strong government facilitation, high social capital among community members, sustained support from non-government organisations (NGOs) or private partners, effective rule enforcement, and the development of viable forest enterprises [@pagdee2006; @blomley2013; @baynes2015]. Where one or more of these conditions are absent, communities may be formally enrolled in CFM programmes without gaining meaningful authority or tangible benefits. Novel revenue streams for ecosystem services, in particular carbon, introduce a whole new set of issues, because of the heightened risks of elite capture and marginalisation of vulnerable community members, and the potentially competing interests among government, developers and community members [@colfer2010b].


Community forestry in Zambia
In Zambia, the trajectory of CFM reflects a gradual transition across four generations of interventions (1980–2025), from early awareness campaigns and tree-planting initiatives to the large-scale adoption of formal community forestry driven largely by REDD+ and carbon finance mechanisms [@moombe2025]. The context for CFM in Zambia is shaped by a distinctive land tenure situation. Although, the Lands Act (1995 amended 2015) nominally invests ownership of land in the President, 94% of the nation’s land is under customary ownership whereby significant land-use decisions reside with traditional chiefs [@sichone2008]. CFM in Zambia, therefore, involves devolution of management authority not only from the state, but also to some extent from traditional leadership. While traditional chiefs are consulted during CFA establishment and remain important community figures, they do not hold explicit management authority within CFMGs — that authority is vested in the elected CFMG executive — and the state through the Forestry Department provides oversight. Moreover, whereas elsewhere CFM has been a critical process in promoting localised resource user rights [@bray2005], these have always been recognised under customary management in Zambia. In contrast, the shift to CFM in Zambia has been driven by a recognition at the national level of a need for sustainable forest management (SFM) to reduce deforestation and forest degradation, while promoting economic development among rural communities. The government estimates that Zambia is currently losing forests at a rate of 250,000 to 300,000 hectares annually, alongside similar amount of biomass lost through forest degradation [@mcnicole2018], making improved forest governance through CFM a national priority aligned with the country’s nationally determined contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. Specifically, Zambia’s NDC 3.0 set a target of 8 million hectares under CFM by 2030, which by January 2025 had already been substantially surpassed.
The legal and policy framework for CFM in Zambia is now well-established. The Forests Act No. 4 of 2015 and the Forests (Community Forest Management) Regulations (SI No. 11 of 2018) provide the principal legal basis for CFM, granting communities the right to apply for recognition as community forest management groups (CFMGs), prepare and implement forest management plans, and access forest user rights including rights to timber, carbon and other ecosystem service revenues. CFM establishment follows a structured seven-step process outlined in the National Guidelines for Community Forestry: (1) Initiation and Awareness, where communities learn about CFM and express interest; (2) Negotiation, Mapping & Signing, where boundaries are agreed and documented with the Forestry Department and traditional leadership; (3) Management Constitution & Election, where the CFMG executive is formally elected (including a Treasurer responsible for financial reporting and accounting) and the CFMG constitution adopted; (4) Management Planning & Rules, where the forest management plan and community forest rules are developed; (5) Agreement Preparation & Signing, where legal agreements between the CFMG and the Forestry Department are formalized; (6) Management Plan Implementation, where the agreed forest management activities begin; and (7) Joint Monitoring, Evaluation & Lesson Learning, where the CFMG’s compliance with the management plan is assessed and performance evaluated. This seven-step process defines the institutional pathway through which customary governance arrangements are formally incorporated into the CFM framework, establishing clear roles, responsibilities, and relationships between the CFMG, the Forestry Department and traditional authorities.








Figure 1: The seven-step CFM establishment process in Zambia, showing the sequential pathway from community awareness through to monitoring and evaluation. Source: National Guidelines for Community Forestry in Zambia (Forestry Department, Zambia, 2018).





Since the formal CFM framework came into effect, the sector has expanded rapidly. The carbon market in particular has accelerated the adoption of CFM in Zambia, offering a vehicle for partnerships between carbon developers, conservation NGOs, and local communities [@moombe2025; @lundu2025; @desouza2026]. As of January 2025, there were 351 CFMGs in Zambia, presiding over approximately 9.4 million hectares of community forests (CFAs) across all ten provinces [@moombe2025]. North-western Province has the largest area under CFM and Luapula the smallest. However, carbon’s role in driving CFM expansion introduces new governance challenges. Carbon projects are typically promoted by carbon developers partnering with communities, creating risks around Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) — community members may be inadequately informed of, or incompletely understand, their contractual obligations under carbon projects or may overestimate the benefits, particularly as these are typically spread over several decades. Moreover, while carbon generates income for CFMGs, this revenue is likely insufficient to realise a community’s aspirations for economic development on its own, potentially setting up a situation where communities become gradually disillusioned with CFM. Large carbon payments also increase risks of irregular benefit-sharing arrangements, elite capture, and disputes over who receives benefits [@desouza2026].
Despite the rapid growth in CFM in Zambia, implementation quality clearly varies considerably. Reflecting patterns in the global picture of CFM implementation, challenges in Zambia include inadequate exit strategies by supporting projects, inconsistent monitoring and follow-up support, low capacity in business and governance skills among CFMGs, insufficient funding to complete the formal establishment process, lack of clarity over benefit-sharing arrangements, poor representation of women despite their high dependence on NTFPs, and unresolved intra- and inter-community conflicts over land and resources [@moombe2022; @lundu2023; @desouza2026].


Aims of the study

Objectives
The objectives of CFM in Zambia, aligned with CFM objectives globally, are twofold: (i) sustainable forest management (SFM) to reduce deforestation and forest degradation while simultaneous generating sustainable yields of forest products; and (ii) sustainable economic development for rural communities. With CFM expanding rapidly in Zambia, the Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ), donors, and other stakeholders have recognised a critical need to understand whether CFM is achieving these intended outcomes, and where improvements in CFM implementation are required. This study was designed to fill that knowledge gap. Specifically, the study aimed to: (i) assess whether CFM in Zambia has led to improved sustainable management of forests; (ii) understand whether CFM has contributed to sustainable development; (iii) identify opportunities for improved implementation of CFM; and (iv) generate policy recommendations to support improved CFM implementation in Zambia.
To address these aims, we surveyed 80 CFMGs across eight provinces (two provinces did not have a sufficient number of CFAs to be included), combining focus group discussions (FGDs) with CFMG executives, female, male and youth community members, and individual interviews with key stakeholders, namely community members, traditional leaders, District Forestry Officers (DFOs), and representatives of private enterprises partnering with CFMGs.
Study structure and the logic of inquiry. The global CFM literature identifies two principal pitfalls that undermine CFM success: (1) weak governance and institutional failure, and (2) failure to develop viable forest enterprises to generate sustainable economic benefits. These pitfalls directly undermine the two primary CFM objectives. To interrogate CFM outcomes against these literature-identified pitfalls, we organised our analysis around four domains:

The Governance domain interrogates the principal literature-identified weak governance pitfall. This chapter assesses whether CFMGs have established functional governance structures, completed legal processes, and implemented financial management and transparency procedures. Critically, we constructed a governance index and used it as a predictor variable to test whether governance quality predicts outcomes across all other domains.
The SFM and Remote Sensing domain directly interrogates the first objective (improved forest management). These chapters assess whether CFMGs are reducing deforestation, managing fire, protecting wildlife, and maintaining forest resources.
The Economic Transformation domain interrogates the second objective (economic development) and directly examines the inadequate enterprise development pitfall. This chapter assesses whether CFMGs have developed viable forest enterprises and whether economic opportunities have materialised for communities.
The Equity and Inclusion domain assesses whether CFM is achieving sustainable development outcomes equitably and captures whether the governance and economic pitfalls differentially affect vulnerable community members.

This analytical approach directly tests whether the literature-identified success conditions (strong governance, viable enterprises, equitable benefit-sharing) are present in Zambia and whether they predict CFM performance. In the last section of the interview tool, we also asked stakeholders how they thought CFM was performing and how they thought it could be improved, which provides additional information on implementation challenges directly from the stakeholders most affected. To address the final aim on providing policy advice, we distilled our findings across the four domains and presented a condensed version of our findings in the Summary and Recommendations chapters that preceded this chapter.


Limitations
An important caveat is that this survey primarily measures perceptions and reported experiences rather than independently verified outcomes. For most findings (governance practices, employment, income changes, forest condition changes), we rely on what community members, CFMG leaders, and other stakeholders told us during interviews and focus group discussions. These perceptions are valuable — communities’ lived experience of CFM is important to understand — but they may differ from objective reality due to social desirability bias (respondents reporting what they want the interviewers to hear), differences in awareness or observation skills, and variation in interpretation of questions. We address these potential biases through the remote sensing chapter, which provides satellite-based verification of key SFM claims, and through triangulation across multiple stakeholder perspectives (comparing what executives, community members, women, youth, and external partners report about the same phenomena). The Methods appendix provides additional detail on assumptions, potential biases, and questionnaire limitations.


Organisation of the report
The remainder of this report is organised as follows. The Survey Overview chapter describes the sample of community forests and interviewees. It demonstrates that the sample is sufficiently representative to support national-level inference. The Governance chapter examines whether CFMGs have completed the required legal and administrative processes, established functional governance structures, and developed business plans. The Sustainable Forest Management chapter assesses the impacts of CFM on deforestation, charcoal production, fire frequency, wildlife, and natural resource management. The Remote Sensing Analysis chapter independently examines the performance of CFM across three SFM indicators: fire incidence, tree canopy cover change and above-ground biomass change. The Economic Transformation chapter evaluates changes in access to forest resources, employment, income, and the realisation of carbon and other economic opportunities. The Equity and Inclusion chapter examines benefit sharing, gender equity, transparency, and the impacts of CFM on poverty. The Discussion chapter summarises the stakeholders’ ideas concerning the performance of CFM implementation and how it can be improved and synthesises findings across all four domains. Four appendices provide supporting material: Appendix I describes the methods in detail; Appendix II contains the full survey tool used in the FGDs and individual interviews; Appendix III provides summary details of the 75 community forests surveyed (five CFAs surveyed were defunct and so removed from the sample); and Appendix IV tabulates the performance indices for governance, SFM, economic transformation and equity & inclusion across all the surveyed CFMGs.

title: Survey overview
text:
Summary
We surveyed 80 CFAs across eight provinces and conducted 549 interviews in total. The sample included CFAs from ~20 ha to >80,000 ha and that varied in years since establishment from one to seven years. In each community forest, we conducted four Focal Group Discussions (FGD, total 292) with (i) the CFMG executive, (ii) community men, (iii) community women, and (iv) community youths. This enabled us to examine differences in perspectives across these groups. In addition, we conducted individual interviews (total = 257) with key stakeholders, including DFOs, CFMG executive members (usually the Secretary), community members, private sector partners including NGOs and for-profit enterprises, and traditional leaders. The same interview tool was used for both FGDs and individual interviews. Overall, the sample was male biased, reflecting gender biases in roles at the community level, but our information is balanced through specifically including a female FGD in each community. The sample included a wide range of ages from ~20 to >80 years. Although most interviewees had lived all their lives in the community, the sample include some who had moved into the community recently. Our sampling approach ensured an unbiased selection and these data demonstrate that we covered a wide range of CFAs, in terms of geography, size and age, and interviewees, in terms of gender, age and roles. Hence, our results may be considered generalisable at the national level.






NoteKey conclusions



The stratified random selection of CFAs, combined with the structured multi-perspective FGD design and the diversity of individual interviewee roles, gender, age and experience, provides a robust foundation for national-level inference about CFM implementation in Zambia. The design is sensitive to within-community heterogeneity, and the geographic and structural breadth of the sample is sufficient to support the conclusions drawn throughout this report.

title: Survey overview
text:
Discussion
This chapter describes the sample of community forests and interviewees that form the basis of all subsequent analyses in this report. The central question for this chapter is whether the sample is sufficiently unbiased and broad to support inferences about CFM implementation at a national level in Zambia.
The selection of CFAs followed a stratified random design: CFAs were randomly selected within each of eight provinces, with a minimum age threshold of one year at the time of sampling. The two provinces omitted — Luapula and Copperbelt — had very few CFAs at the time of the survey, and therefore their exclusion does not compromise national representativeness. Five CFAs included in the original sample could not be surveyed after it became clear they existed only on paper. The final sample of 75 CFAs is provided in Appendix III. The sample spans a wide range of CFA sizes and ages: from very small CFAs of around 20 ha to large ones exceeding 80,000 ha, and from newly established CFAs of one year to approximately seven years old. Because the CFM programme only received enabling regulations in 2018, most CFAs in Zambia are fewer than three years old, and our sample reflects this age structure appropriately. Together, the geographic and structural breadth of the sample supports the conclusion that it is representative of the national CFA population.
The multi-perspective FGD design is the key methodological feature that enables meaningful inference from interview data. By conducting four structured FGDs per CFA — with the CFMG executive committee, community men, community women, and community youth — the survey is able to capture systematically divergent perspectives within each community. The near-complete coverage of all four FGD types across the 75 CFAs means that differences in responses among these groups, which feature prominently throughout the report, can be interpreted with confidence.
Individual interviews were targeted at five key stakeholder roles: CFMG executive members, DFOs, traditional leaders, forest user-group chairs, and external partners. Not all roles were available at every CFA, which introduces some variation in coverage, but the sample sizes for each category are sufficient for quantitative analyses of the responses.
The gender breakdown of interviewees reflects real-world patterns: men dominate most CFMG stakeholder roles, and so the overall sample is male-biased. However, the dedicated female FGD in each CFA and the inclusion of female individual interviewees where available ensure that women’s perspectives are not lost. The age structure and ‘years living in the community’ of interviewees suggest a broadly representative sample of community members, spanning both recent arrivals and long-term residents across all provinces. The years of CFMG involvement reported by interviewees are consistent with the age of the programme, and where involvement exceeds seven years it likely reflects participation in predecessor community resource management structures, such as CRBs.
In conclusion, the stratified random selection of CFAs, combined with the structured multi-perspective FGD design and the diversity of individual interviewee roles, gender, age and experience, provides a robust foundation for national-level inference about CFM implementation in Zambia.

title: Governance
text:
Summary
The implementation of CFM processes is patchy. The legal processes required for establishment of a CFA were mostly complete across our sample, but later processes such as the registration certificate, forest-use permits and benefit-sharing agreement have not been completed for a substantial number of CFAs. While most CFMGs have held elections, have term-limits for executive officers and hold meetings with reasonable frequency, a large proportion have not opened a bank account, do not have a receipt book and have not completed annual financial and technical reports. Most CFMGs are overdue elections and hence are not compliant with their By-laws & Constitutions. This is particularly worrying as, in some cases, it may reflect an attempt by CFMG executives to retain control for personal benefit. Business processes are even less well implemented. Many do not have a business plan, annual budgets or workplans. Many also do not have defined user groups or issue permits. Most CFMGs are only rarely visited by district forestry staff, but most are supported by conservation NGOs or carbon developers, who do visit more frequently. The frequency of visits by district forestry staff was significantly associated with a higher governance index score. Interest in expanding the CFA was highest among CFMG executives and lowest among community youth, while among individual interview respondents, private enterprise representatives indicated they would like to expand the CFA significantly more often than traditional leaders (usually headmen or headwomen) and community members. The governance index was a highly significant indicator of community interest in expanding the CFA, an indicator of satisfaction with CFM. Thus, conversely, poor governance constitutes a risk to the sustainability of CFM in Zambia.






NoteKey conclusions



CFMG governance is patchy. There are some areas of serious concern. The legal framework for CFM is in place across most CFMGs, but institutional and business management processes lag behind. Many CFMGs are not in compliance with their own by-laws and constitutions, with respect to annual reporting and term limits for executive officers. Oversight of CFM is a statutory duty of the FD, but visits from district forestry office staff are often rare to non-existent. Higher visit frequency from district forestry staff was a significant predictor of better governance. Improving governance, primarily through strengthening financial management and CFMG democratic processes by expanding district forestry staff engagement, will be essential for CFM to fulfil its potential in Zambia.

title: Governance
text:
Introduction
In this chapter, we consider questions concerning the governance and management of CFMGs. As our questions pertain to the running of the CFMGs, our analysis focuses on the responses of the CFMG executives. However, the responses from other FGDs and from the individual interviews are included for comparison where appropriate.
We examine the hypothesis that CFMGs with stronger governance — completing legal requirements, maintaining transparent financial records, holding regular elections, and making decisions transparently — would be more successful at protecting their forests and generating economic benefits for their communities, thereby generating greater community support for CFM. We test this by examining the completion of governance processes, comparing these results across CFMGs, and interrogating community groups as to whether they would support expansion of the CFA, as an indicator of satisfaction with CFM. In later chapters, we assess whether better governance predicts better outcomes for forest management and economic development.

title: Governance
text:
Discussion
In this chapter we assessed CFMG governance across five domains: legal processes, governance processes, business processes, external support, and community buy-in as reflected by interest in expanding the CFA and the activities of user-groups.
The most consistent pattern across all three process domains — legal, governance, and business — is that foundational steps have been taken by most CFMGs, but the more demanding, ongoing requirements are often incomplete. Early legal steps, such as obtaining a recognition letter and signing a forest management agreement, have been completed by most CFMGs, but later and more involved documents — the registration certificate, forest-use permit, and benefit-sharing agreement — are absent in a substantial proportion. Similarly with respect to governance processes, most CFMGs have held elections and have term limits in place, but basic management actions — opening bank accounts, operating receipt books, and financial and annual reporting — are frequently missing. Business processes are the weakest area of all. Annual workplans, budgets and business plans are rarely in place. Without these planning and financial management tools, CFMGs cannot sustainably manage their resources, are poorly positioned to account for and redistribute income — including carbon payments — and will struggle to demonstrate compliance with the forest management license or to agreements with external partners.
The fact that most CFMGs are overdue for elections is particularly concerning. Timely elections are a basic requirement of the CFMG By-laws & Constitution, and overdue elections undermine the democratic legitimacy of the CFMG executives and could contribute to the perception of elite capture noted elsewhere in this report. These perceptions may be very valid in some cases. The enumerators noted that while some CFMGs had not held elections because they were no longer active, the CFMG executives of others stated that the CFMG had yet to receive carbon income and they were unwilling to hold elections, because they anticipated personal benefits from being a CFMG executive member once the carbon income started to flow. Still others had received carbon income and were unwilling to give up their positions because they do receive some kind of personal benefit. It is essential that this kind of corruption is stamped out, as it may threaten the legitimacy of CFM in the eyes of the community and potentially undo gains made in SFM and sustainable development. Ensuring that CFMGs hold elections on schedule and fairly should be a priority for the FD and for supporting partners.
External support from the FD is insufficient. Most CFMGs are rarely or never visited by district forestry staff, despite the statutory duty of the FD to implement the CFM policy. This gap is partly compensated by conservation NGOs and carbon developers, many of which visit their partner CFMGs more frequently. However, this support is not universal: a significant proportion of CFMGs in our sample had no external partner. Given the governance deficits identified above, regular external support from CFMG partners for capacity building and oversight is clearly a necessity. The current model, in which CFM is effectively co-governed by the community and the private sector rather than the state, may be adequate for CFMGs with active and capable partners, but leaves others without meaningful support. It is noteworthy that, according to the analysis of our Governance Index, frequency of visits from district forestry staff was a highly significant predictor of governance performance.
Interest in expanding the CFA is highest among CFMG executives and drops markedly among community members, particularly youth. Among individual interviewees, Private enterprise reps are significantly more enthusiastic about expansion than traditional leaders or community members. This divergence — consistent with the equity chapter findings — suggests that the CFMG leadership and external partner stakeholders have a more optimistic view of CFM outcomes than the broader community. Furthermore, we found that our governance index was a highly significant predictor of community interest in expanding the CFA, which we take as a proxy indicator for satisfaction with CFM. Thus, as we hypothesised, when CFMGs are better governed there is greater community support for CFM. Thus, conversely, poor governance could lead to increased levels of community dissatisfaction with CFM and, if not addressed, could pose a long-term risk to the legitimacy and sustainability of CFM in Zambia.

text: Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?

title: Sustainable Forest Management
text:
Summary
Most FGD respondents indicated that deforestation, charcoal production and fire frequency were decreasing and wildlife populations were increasing with their CFAs, and that natural resource management was improving within their CFAs. In addition, most FGD groups indicated that both deforestation and charcoal production were decreasing outside their CFA, suggesting there is no leakage or potentially a positive leakage effect. Community female FGDs tended to have a more positive view of the impact of CFM on SFM compared to the other groups, which is noteworthy given it is primarily the women who harvest forest products, but who often do not have voice in traditional natural resource management. However, it is also important to note that for a minority of CFAs both FGD groups and individual interviewees suggested the situation was worsening. Moreover, the governance index was a significant predictor of our SFM performance index. Very few CFMGs were practising restoration or establishing plantations. Existing CFAs should be expanded and new ones designed so that they incorporate degraded areas and contribute to national restoration and plantation targets. While most community groups felt SFM indicators were improving under CFM, it is important to identify those CFAs that are failing and address the causes, which our results suggest are likely to be linked to poor governance.






NoteKey conclusions



According to the perceptions expressed by the FGDs, CFM in Zambia is improving SFM across a substantial majority of surveyed communities, with positive spillover effects in the surrounding landscape and encouraging indications of women’s engagement in forest governance. However, the survey identified a minority of CFAs in which the situation was worsening and the governance index was a significant predictor of SFM performance. The identified link between governance quality and SFM performance is critical and underscores the need for improving governance across the CFM portfolio. Zambia could also benefit from a systematic approach to restoration and plantation through CFM.
